places.name: Where the valley begins
places.text: At the foot of the Grapevine, the freeway reaches the southern tip of the San Joaquin Valley, about 1,500 feet above sea level. Between Tejon Pass and here, the road changes elevation by more than 2,600 feet in about 12 miles. From here the Central Valley, broad and flat, runs about 450 miles between the Coast Ranges and the Sierra Nevada.
places.more: The whole Central Valley is 40 to 60 miles wide and covers about 18,000 square miles, about 11 percent of California. Geologists think it began below sea level, as an offshore basin, and it has no earthquake faults of its own, though faults surround it on both sides. This southern end, the Tulare Basin, has a semi-arid desert climate. Before farming, it was desert grassland, with marshes, big lakes such as Tulare, Buena Vista and Kern, and herds of tule elk and pronghorn. Today only about 1 percent of the valley's original grassland is intact, and more than 7 million acres are irrigated.
places.spot: Look for the place where steep mountains meet the flat valley floor.

places.name: Water lifted over the mountains
places.text: About 6 miles east of here, the Edmonston Pumping Plant lifts California Aqueduct water 1,926 feet up and over the Tehachapi Mountains toward Southern California. Apart from pumped-storage power plants, it is the most powerful water-lifting system in the world. At full capacity its pumps can send nearly 2 million gallons a minute uphill.
places.more: It has 14 pumps. Each motor and pump unit stands 65 feet tall and weighs 420 tons, and the pumps reach six floors down. Two pipes 12.5 to 14 feet across climb the mountain inside a tunnel 8,400 feet long, and each always holds 8.5 million gallons of water. At the top, a surge tank 68 feet tall keeps sudden valve changes from damaging the tunnel. Running every pump takes up to 787 megawatts of electricity, delivered on its own power line. Over the top, the aqueduct splits into West and East Branches. Before reaching Edmonston, the water climbs in steps at three earlier plants: Buena Vista, Teerink and Chrisman.

places.name: Wheeler Ridge, a growing fold
places.text: The long, low ridge where the mountains meet the valley floor here is Wheeler Ridge, a fold in the earth's crust that is still growing. It is being pushed up over a thrust fault, and geologists have found that the fold is getting longer at its eastern end, toward the east-southeast.
places.more: The evidence is written in the land. Streams that cross the eastern end of the ridge bend toward the east-southeast, deflected as the rising rock grows in front of them. On the crest sits a wind gap, an old stream channel left high and dry, at the same height as the canyon a nearby stream uses today, a sign that the stream was pushed aside as the ridge rose. The ridge is also lower toward its eastern end, and its soils there are younger than in the west. It belongs to the Pleito-Wheeler Ridge thrust fault system, which has been active since the late Pleistocene. The White Wolf Fault, which caused the 1952 earthquake, may merge with the Pleito thrust fault at its southwestern end.
places.spot: Look for the long, low ridge rising where the mountains meet the valley floor.

places.name: Start of the West Side Freeway
places.text: Highway 99 and I-5 meet at the Wheeler Ridge interchange. From here to Woodland, I-5 is the West Side Freeway. It was chosen as the Interstate route because it skips the valley's big cities, such as Bakersfield and Fresno, for a faster, more direct trip. The section between here and Los Banos opened in 1972.
places.more: Local groups pushed for a west side freeway as early as 1945, and when the Interstate system was created in 1956, it won out over turning Highway 99 into the Interstate. Construction began in the early 1960s in just three phases covering 321 miles: the San Joaquin County line to Los Banos by 1967, this stretch by 1972, and the link to Sacramento by 1979. When this section opened, it was a long, lonely road with no businesses beside it, and the nearest towns were miles away and usually out of sight. Running out of gas was common. Travel stops grew up at the exits over the years. The wide median between Wheeler Ridge and Tracy leaves room to widen the freeway to six or eight lanes someday.
places.spot: Look for the big interchange where Highway 99 and I-5 meet.

places.name: The 1952 earthquake
places.text: At 4:52 in the morning on July 21, 1952, the White Wolf Fault broke near Wheeler Ridge in a magnitude 7.3 earthquake, the strongest in California since 1906. It killed 12 people, and the mountain town of Tehachapi was hit hardest. Out in the valley fields, rows of cotton were found shifted sideways, one of them by 3 feet.
places.more: The White Wolf Fault is about 56 miles long, and the shaking started at its southwestern end, near here. Southeast of Bealville, railroad tunnels with concrete walls 18 inches thick cracked, and the gap between two tunnel entrances shrank by up to 8 feet. A crew of a thousand workers reopened the line in 25 days. A month later, on August 22, a magnitude 5.8 aftershock badly damaged brick buildings in downtown Bakersfield and killed two more people. Afraid of more shaking, many families slept outdoors, where mosquitoes bit them and spread encephalitis that summer. The same fault shook Wheeler Ridge again in 2005, with a magnitude 5.2 quake.

places.name: James Dean's speeding ticket
places.text: On September 30, 1955, the actor James Dean was driving north on Highway 99, on his way to a sports car race in Salinas, when a Highway Patrol officer pulled him over near here and wrote him a speeding ticket. The officer listed the place as Mettler Station. Later that same day, Dean was killed in a crash farther along his trip.
places.more: Dean was 24 and had made only three major films: East of Eden, Rebel Without a Cause, and Giant, which came out after his death. He got serious about racing in 1954 and placed in several big events in a Porsche Speedster, but the director of Giant barred him from racing during filming. Once his scenes were done, he traded the Speedster for a new, more powerful Porsche 550 Spyder and entered the Salinas Road Race for October 2. A mechanic, a photographer and a stunt coordinator traveled with him, and the stunt coordinator, following in another car, got a speeding ticket too. The officer who wrote Dean's ticket, at about 3:30 in the afternoon, was O. V. Hunter of the California Highway Patrol. Mettler itself is a tiny place, founded by the Mettler family in the 1940s.

places.name: The Lakeview Gusher
places.text: Near Maricopa, in March 1910, an oil well called Lakeview Number One blew out and would not stop. For 18 months it gushed, about 9 million barrels in all, and it is often called the largest accidental oil spill in history. The force of the flow destroyed the derrick.
places.more: The Lakeview Oil Company began drilling on New Year's Day 1909, and legend says the spot was chosen because clumps of red grass were thought to mean oil. At first the crew found only gas, the company ran out of money, and it teamed up with Union Oil. Wells then had no blowout preventers like those used today, and at about 2,440 feet down, oil burst through the casing. Workers threw up sandbag dams and dikes to hold back a river of crude and piped some of it to tanks 2.5 miles away, saving about 40 percent. The glut cut oil prices to about 30 cents a barrel, roughly half the earlier price. It never caught fire. A state landmark plaque marks the site off Highway 33.

places.name: Wind Wolves Preserve
places.text: In the hills southwest of here lies Wind Wolves Preserve, 93,000 acres of grassland, oak and canyon that its owner, The Wildlands Conservancy, calls the largest nonprofit nature preserve on the West Coast. The name describes tall grass bending and parting in gusts of wind, like unseen animals running across the slopes. In 1998, 19 tule elk were released here, and the herd has grown to about 500.
places.more: The land climbs from about 640 feet to more than 6,000 feet, through grassland, oak savanna, pinyon and juniper, and conifer forest. It is part of the homeland of Chumash, Yokuts and Kitanemuk peoples. At Pleito, a Chumash rock art site in the preserve, researchers have studied the fragile paintings with portable X-ray instruments and 3D scanning, methods that leave the paint untouched. The land was part of the 1842 Mexican land grant Rancho San Emidio and was a cattle ranch until the 1990s. California condors forage over it, and in 2015 thousands of tricolored blackbirds nested here. Since 1996, more than 157,000 Kern County students have come for outdoor classes, and a spring nature festival brings guided hikes and wildflower viewing.

places.name: Mountains named for a saint
places.text: The mountains forming the valley's southern wall are the San Emigdio Mountains, which top out at 7,492 feet. They are named for Saint Emygdius, an early Christian martyr whom Catholics call on for protection from earthquakes. It suits them: their eastern end reaches Lebec, near where the San Andreas and Garlock faults come together.
places.more: Emygdius was a bishop in Ascoli Piceno, Italy. In 1703 a violent earthquake shook the region but spared the city, people gave him the credit, and from then on he was invoked against earthquakes. All Catholic churches in California are directed to mark his feast day and ask his protection from earthquakes. The range links the Tehachapi Mountains with the Temblor Range, whose own name is Spanish for tremor. Its highest peaks include San Emigdio Mountain, Tecuya Mountain and Brush Mountain, all above 7,000 feet. San Emigdio Creek, which runs year-round, carries the same name down San Emigdio Canyon.
places.spot: Look for the long wall of mountains along the south edge of the valley.

places.name: El Camino Viejo, the Old Road
places.text: Long before this freeway, an older road ran along the west side of the valley. El Camino Viejo, the Old Road to Los Angeles, came over Tejon Pass, down through the San Emigdio Mountains to Buena Vista Lake, then north along the foothills from one watering place to the next, all the way to San Francisco Bay. Spanish ox carts used it as early as 1780.
places.more: It was the oldest north-south trail in the interior of Spanish and Mexican California. Coming from Tejon Pass, it avoided Grapevine Canyon, turning west up Cuddy Canyon and coming down San Emigdio Creek into the valley, past Rancho San Emidio, a land grant of 1842. In the 1840s, more Mexican land grant ranchos were set up along the route. The names of its Kern County stops describe this country: Aguaje de la Brea, the tar watering place; Aguaje de los Temblores, the watering place of the earthquakes; and Aguaje Mesteño, the mustang watering place. Farther north came Arroyo de las Polvarduras, the creek of the dust storms, and Arroyo Pasajero, the travelers' creek.

places.name: Kern Lake's empty bed
places.text: The flat fields near the freeway here were once Kern Lake, the smallest of three big lakes at the south end of the valley. It was the first lake the Kern River fed. From Kern Lake, water ran west through a channel called Connecting Slough into Buena Vista Lake, and in wet years the two joined into one large lake. Diverting the river for farms in the 1800s left it a dry bed.
places.more: The southern end of the valley is a basin with no regular outlet to the sea. When Kern and Buena Vista lakes filled up together, the overflow ran north through the Buena Vista Slough, tule marshes and Goose Lake into Tulare Lake, the largest of all. Tulare Lake in turn spilled north into the San Joaquin River in 19 of the 29 years from 1850 to 1878, but never again after that. All three lakes were remnants of a far bigger one, Lake Corcoran, which covered the Central Valley until about 600,000 years ago, when a new outlet broke through at San Francisco Bay and drained it.

places.name: Kern County nut country
places.text: Many of the neat rows of trees in Kern County are almonds and pistachios. In 2022 the county harvested about 223,000 acres of almonds and 158,000 acres of pistachios, more pistachio acres than any other county in California. Together those two nuts were worth about 1.6 billion dollars that year, and California grows 99 percent of the country's pistachios.
places.more: Pistachio trees are either male or female, and only females bear nuts; one male tree makes enough pollen for 8 to 12 females. The trees take 7 to 10 years to reach real production and bear heavier crops in alternate years. Kern's pistachio harvest went from about 252,000 tons in 2021 to 146,000 in 2022. California's first commercial pistachio harvest came only in 1976. For all those nuts, Kern's most valuable farm product in 2022 was grapes, mostly table grapes, followed by citrus, almonds and milk, and in 2013 the county grew about 80 percent of the country's carrots. Farming nuts here takes a lot of water: an acre of pistachios can use more than a million gallons a year.
places.spot: Look for orchards of almond or pistachio trees planted in long, straight rows.

places.name: Buena Vista Lake
places.text: Southwest of here, much of the farmland was once Buena Vista Lake, fed by the Kern River and the second largest of the lakes in the Tulare Basin. On its south shore stood Tulamniu, a Yokuts village lived in for several centuries, which the Spanish commander Pedro Fages named Buena Vista in 1772. Two small lakes, Lake Webb and Lake Evans, now sit on part of the old bed.
places.more: The village's people spoke Buena Vista Yokuts. The Spanish priest Father Zalvidea recorded the site again in 1806, and in 1933 and 1934 the Smithsonian Institution excavated it; it is now California Historical Landmark 374. Later the cattle company Miller and Lux owned the lakebed, and Henry Miller's heirs sold it to the J. G. Boswell Company. Lake Webb and Lake Evans were created in 1973 for recreation, and together they hold about 6,800 acre-feet of Kern River water. In June 2023, after a snowpack three times normal in the southern Sierra, the Kern River began to refill the top of the old lake, to a depth of a few feet.

places.name: Taft, once called Moron
places.text: Highway 119 leads to Taft, an oil town at the valley's southwest edge. The town's oil museum tells how locals asked the railroad to name its station Moro, but the railroad worried it would be confused with Morro Bay and named it Moron instead, back when the word did not yet mean anything unkind. In 1909 the town took a new name, for President William Howard Taft.
places.more: Taft began as Siding Number Two on the Sunset Railroad, which was built to carry crude oil out and bring drinking water in. It is one of the few towns in the country that exist only because of nearby oil. The Midway-Sunset field around it has produced nearly 4 billion barrels of crude, and at one time as many as 6,000 people in Taft reportedly worked for Standard Oil. The president it is named for also set aside the nearby Elk Hills as the Navy's first oil reserve, in 1912. As of 2015, Kern County had 78 percent of California's active oil wells. In the middle of town, a bronze monument 37 feet tall shows oil workers on a derrick, and the West Kern Oil Museum keeps a historic wooden derrick.

places.name: Crossing the Kern River
places.text: The freeway crosses the Kern River here, though this far downstream its channel is often dry. John C. Frémont named the river in 1845 for Edward Kern, the mapmaker of his expedition, who, as the story goes, nearly drowned in its rushing water. Long before that, in 1776, the Spanish missionary Francisco Garcés had called it the Río de San Felipe.
places.more: The Kern starts high in the Sierra Nevada northwest of Mount Whitney and drops through a deep canyon to Bakersfield. Almost all its water is now diverted for farms, towns and groundwater banks, and in 2022 the group American Rivers listed the lower Kern among America's most endangered rivers because its last 25 miles had dried up. In flood years, a weir lets extra water spill into the California Aqueduct, and the rest runs south toward the old Buena Vista lakebed. Before Frémont, people locally called it Po-sun-co-la, and floods often shifted its channel. Accounts say the great earthquake of 1857 briefly made the river flow backward.
places.spot: Look for the Kern River's channel passing under the freeway.

places.name: Kern Water Bank
places.text: Near here, the Kern Water Bank covers about 32 square miles of the southern San Joaquin Valley. In wet years, water is spread into more than 80 basins and slowly soaks into the ground, where it is saved for dry years. It can store 1.5 million acre-feet underground, more than two and a half times what Lake Isabella, the big reservoir upriver, can hold.
places.more: About 8,800 acres of the bank are recharge basins, and 91 wells pump the water back up when it is needed. When the basins fill in wet years they look like lakes, and wildlife moves in. The bank's general manager has counted 240 kinds of birds there and as many as 35,000 water birds, and an endangered plant called San Joaquin woolly threads grows on the bank. It takes in water from the Kern River and from the state and federal water projects. It is a public-private partnership, and the largest share, 57 percent, is controlled by Stewart and Lynda Resnick, owners of brands including Pom Wonderful and Halos.

places.name: Elk Hills and Teapot Dome
places.text: The low hills to the west are the Elk Hills, over one of the most productive oil fields in the country. In 1912 President Taft made them the nation's first Naval Petroleum Reserve, oil saved for the Navy. In 1922 Interior Secretary Albert Fall leased them, without competitive bidding, to oilman Edward Doheny, who had quietly lent Fall 100,000 dollars with no interest. The deal became part of the Teapot Dome scandal.
places.more: In 1927 the Supreme Court ruled the lease had been corruptly obtained and gave the hills back to the Navy. Convicted in 1929 of taking bribes from Doheny, Fall became the first Cabinet member to go to prison, while Doheny was acquitted of paying them. Doheny's company even foreclosed on Fall's home in New Mexico over that same 100,000 dollar loan. The oil stayed mostly in the ground until the oil embargo of the 1970s, and production peaked in 1981, when one oil pool alone yielded 42 million barrels. In 1997 the government sold the reserve to Occidental Petroleum, the highest bidder. The field has produced close to 1.5 billion barrels of oil.
places.spot: Look for long, low, bare hills along the west side of the valley.

places.name: Tule Elk State Natural Reserve
places.text: A few miles southwest, Tule Elk State Natural Reserve keeps a herd of about 30 to 35 tule elk on nearly 1,000 acres, watched from a viewing platform. These elk are found only in California. About half a million once roamed the state, but by the 1870s they were thought to be extinct, until a few were found hiding in the tules near Buena Vista Lake.
places.more: In 1874, a tip from the cattle baron Henry Miller led game warden A. C. Tibbets to the survivors, and Miller protected them on his land; an 1895 count found just 28. Genetic studies suggest that at the low point, as few as two or three elk may have been breeding. The reserve was established in 1932 as the Tupman Zoological Reserve, and elk from here have helped start other herds, including those in the Owens Valley and near San Luis Obispo. About 5,700 tule elk roam California again. The elk are most active from late summer through early autumn. Summer is their mating season, when temperatures here can top 110 degrees, and the park suggests bringing binoculars.

places.name: Henry Miller, the Cattle King
places.text: Buttonwillow was a headquarters of Miller and Lux, the company of Henry Miller, known as the Cattle King of California. Miller came west in 1850 as a butcher and teamed up with another German immigrant, Charles Lux, in 1858. At its height the company owned about 1.4 million acres outright and controlled nearly 22,000 square miles of land in California, Nevada and Oregon.
places.more: He was born Heinrich Kreiser in Germany. In New York he bought a friend's steamship ticket to California that could not be transferred to anyone else, so he traveled under the name printed on it, Henry Miller, and kept it for life. Miller and Lux bought up Spanish and Mexican land grants for about 1.15 dollars an acre and became the largest cattle producer in California, and Miller managed it closely through detailed letters to his superintendents. He was said to keep local officials, especially county assessors, in his debt. Some of his descendants still farm around Los Banos and in Kern County. When Miller died in 1916, his estate was appraised at about 40 million dollars.

places.name: The Buttonwillow tree
places.text: The town of Buttonwillow is named for a single tree, and it is not a willow at all. It is a buttonbush. A lone one here stood out as a landmark on an old trail across the valley, and it was a Yokuts meeting place long before settlers held stock rodeos beside it. The tree is now California Historical Landmark 492.
places.more: Around 1885 the cattle company Miller and Lux set up its headquarters and store beside the tree. When the town was founded in 1895 it was first called Buena Vista, but the name quickly became Buttonwillow. Cotton farming is its main industry, and locals call this cotton country. About 1,300 people live here, and for drivers it is a major stop, with gas stations, restaurants and travel centers at the Highway 58 exit. Buttonwillow Raceway Park nearby hosts sports car club races, and every year model jet fans gather here for a rally called Best in the West.

places.name: California's balance point
places.text: About 7 miles northeast of here lies the center of population of California. The Census Bureau finds it by imagining a flat, weightless map of the state with every resident given the same weight, then finding the point where the map would balance. Since 1970, that point has stayed within about 10 miles of Buttonwillow.
places.more: The Census Bureau's table for California begins in 1880, when the center lay west of Stockton, more than 200 miles to the northwest. Over the following decades it slid south down the valley: to southwestern Fresno County by 1920, north of Lost Hills by 1930, and into this part of Kern County by 1960. In 1960 and 1970 it lay less than a mile from where this freeway now runs. Since then it has wandered only a few miles, staying east of Buttonwillow, and in 2020 it landed between Buttonwillow and Shafter.

places.name: Midway Substation
places.text: The big electrical yard about a mile east of Buttonwillow is Midway Substation. Here Southern California Edison's power lines, which cross the mountains to the south, meet PG&E's grid. In winter, power often flows north toward the Pacific Northwest, where people run heaters; in summer it flows south for air conditioners.
places.more: Midway is the southern end of Path 15, part of the Pacific AC Intertie. The intertie was built in the 1970s and 1980s so California and the Southwest could use extra hydropower from the Northwest without building new power plants. Midway is also the northern end of Path 26, three Edison lines of 500,000 volts that cross the Tehachapi Mountains toward the Antelope Valley. Two big lines from the Diablo Canyon Power Plant on the coast cross the coastal mountains to reach Midway. A set of smaller 230,000-volt lines runs alongside the main ones.
places.spot: Look for rows of giant steel power towers marching across the fields.

places.name: McKittrick Tar Pits
places.text: West of Buttonwillow, near the tiny town of McKittrick, natural asphalt oozes out of the ground from the oil field below. Like the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles, these pits trapped animals during the ice ages, from about 15,000 to 50,000 years ago. Fossils found here include saber-toothed cats, short-faced bears, American lions, ground sloths, bison and mammoths.
places.more: The pits are counted among only five natural asphalt lake areas in the world, and three of those are in California: here, La Brea and Carpinteria. They stretch over about 4 miles. Yokuts people mined the asphalt and used it to waterproof things, for decoration and for trade, and settlers began mining it in the 1860s. University of California scientists dug here in 1928, and the excavation was finished in 1949 by the Los Angeles and Kern County museums. By 1968, more than 43 kinds of mammals and 58 kinds of birds had been identified. The town is named for Captain William McKittrick, a local landowner and rancher, and about 100 people live there.

places.name: Cotton country
places.text: Cotton has deep roots on this side of the valley. Sandy loam soils, a long growing season without rain, big irrigation systems and relative freedom from pests like the boll weevil made the San Joaquin Valley ideal cotton land. A strain called Acala, developed at the cotton research station in nearby Shafter, became so important that state laws passed in 1925 made it the only cotton allowed in key areas.
places.more: The one-variety rule kept the cotton from cross-pollinating and helped sell it. Production grew fast in the 1930s, and by 1970 cotton was California's leading cash crop. In 1933, more than 18,000 cotton pickers in the southern valley, mostly Mexican migrant workers, went on strike, and 3,500 of them lived in a four-acre camp outside Corcoran. In the end the federal government stepped in to force both sides to negotiate. After World War II, mechanical pickers sharply cut the need for hand labor. After 2000, cotton declined as new insect pests arrived and other crops paid better, but Kings County, to the north, is still California's top cotton county, growing mostly Pima cotton.

places.name: The Temblor Range
places.text: On clear days, the mountains along the far western skyline are the Temblor Range, named from the Spanish word for tremor. The San Andreas Fault runs along the foot of their far side, at the edge of the Carrizo Plain. The peaks average about 3,500 feet, and the highest, McKittrick Summit, reaches 4,331 feet.
places.more: The range is young: it rose mostly within the last few million years, pushed up by the San Andreas and other faults. Its rocks hold marine fossils, because seawater once covered this end of the valley. Sometime in the last 1.8 million years, a block of shale more than 6 miles long, a mile wide and over 2,000 feet thick slid down the range's northeastern side, traveled about 3 miles and buried the McKittrick oil field. Highway 58 crosses the range at 3,750 feet, and Highway 46 uses its lowest pass, Polonio Pass, at 1,750 feet.
places.spot: Look for a long line of mountains far off on the western skyline.

places.name: San Joaquin kit fox
places.text: This dry west side of the valley is home to the San Joaquin kit fox, an endangered fox with huge ears. Kit foxes are the smallest wild members of the dog family in North America, and an adult weighs only about 5 pounds. It hunts mostly at night, mainly for kangaroo rats.
places.more: It was once common across the San Joaquin Valley, but by 1930 its range had shrunk by more than half. Today its largest populations live in western Kern County, in and around the Elk Hills and the Buena Vista Valley. Its dens are deep, with several openings, which help it escape the heat and its enemies. Kit foxes even live in Bakersfield, where rat poisons and a mange outbreak first seen in 2013 are serious threats. It is protected under the federal endangered species law of 1966, the forerunner of today's Endangered Species Act.

places.name: Downhill all the way
places.text: A few miles west, the California Aqueduct flows downhill by gravity, with no pumps. From the Coastal Branch split south of Kettleman City, its water runs about 66 miles to the Buena Vista Pumping Plant, the first of four plants that lift it toward and over the Tehachapi Mountains. The canal is built on a slight grade so gravity does the work.
places.more: The town of Lost Hills stands on the aqueduct's east bank. The aqueduct carries water for about 35 million people and 5.7 million acres of farmland, and farming on the West Side grew quickly after it was finished in the early 1970s. But pumping groundwater has made land along parts of the canal sink. By the 1970s some areas of the valley had dropped as much as 28 feet, and NASA's GRACE satellites measure the Tulare Basin sinking about a foot a year. A sagging canal carries less water and costs more to run.

places.name: Blackwells Corner
places.text: West on Highway 46, where it meets Highway 33, Blackwells Corner is named for George Blackwell, who started a rest stop there in 1921. On September 30, 1955, James Dean stopped there on his way to a race in Salinas, and it is often described as the last place he was seen alive before his fatal crash near Cholame.
places.more: Dean was driving west on what was then Highway 466, now Highway 46. At about 5:45 that evening, near Cholame, a college student driving the other way turned left across his path toward Highway 41, and Dean could not stop in time. The death certificate placed the crash one mile east of Cholame, at the junction of Highways 466 and 41, and an inquest jury found no criminal act. In 1977 a Japanese businessman, Seita Ohnishi, brought a stainless-steel memorial, built in Japan, to Cholame, where it stands in front of the old post office.

places.name: Lost Hills
places.text: Lost Hills, a town of about 2,400 people a couple of miles west of the freeway, takes its name from the low Lost Hills range beside it. Many residents work for the Wonderful Company, whose pistachio and almond processing plant is here. Each fall, pistachio trees are shaken and the nuts hauled to processing plants; at the one in Lost Hills, workers sort them by hand.
places.more: After a pedestrian was killed crossing Highway 46, the Wonderful Company paid for a green footbridge over the highway. It is shaped like a lizard, and it funnels rain that lands on it to the sides so the water can be collected. The town's post office opened in 1911, and at one time it was a small rented room in Edmondson's cafe and bar. In the early 2000s, a company called Paramount Farms built a new park and housing here. California's pistachio crop was worth nearly 3 billion dollars in 2023, and the United States has passed Iran as the world's top exporter of the nut.

places.name: Lost Hills oil field
places.text: In July 1910, two drillers named Martin and Dudley were drilling a water well for livestock in the low hills west of here. At 530 feet they struck oil instead, and the Lost Hills oil field was born. The hills rise barely 200 feet above the valley, and so much oil has been pumped out that parts of them have sunk as much as 8 feet.
places.more: In 1998 the field was the site of the Bellevue blowout, one of the most spectacular well blowouts in modern U.S. history. On the evening of November 23, a wildcat well northeast of the main field reached 17,000 feet and hit gas under enormous pressure. It burst into flame, knocked over the drilling rig and melted nearby equipment, and the pillar of fire, about 340 feet tall, could be seen more than 40 miles away. It burned for 14 days, and gas kept escaping for about six months, until crews drilled a second, slanted hole to meet the well deep underground and plug it. The sinking ground causes trouble too: in 1976 a Getty Oil well collapsed into a crater more than 15 feet deep, taking its concrete pad and pump with it.

places.name: Tule fog season
places.text: From November through March, tule fog can fill this southern end of the valley. The thick ground fog, named for the tule marshes of the Central Valley, tends to last longer in the south and east of the valley than farther north. Inside it, visibility is usually less than 600 feet, and it can drop to almost nothing within a few feet.
places.more: It forms on long, calm nights after a good rain, when the damp ground cools. Tule fog is a low cloud, usually below 2,000 feet, trapped by the mountains around the valley and pressed down by warmer air above, and it can linger for days or even weeks. Drive up into the foothills and you can look down on it from mild, clear air. As of 2005 it was the leading cause of weather-related accidents in California. In January 2024, fog led to a pileup of more than 40 vehicles on I-5 in Kern County that killed two people. When it forms, slow down and leave plenty of room.

places.name: Kern National Wildlife Refuge
places.text: East of here, Kern National Wildlife Refuge protects 11,249 acres of desert uplands, an old river corridor and marsh on the southern edge of what was once Tulare Lake. In winter its wetlands shelter migrating ducks, geese and other water birds that travel the Pacific Flyway.
places.more: The refuge was set aside on November 18, 1960. Besides its marshes, it protects a remnant of the valley's original desert uplands and habitat for several endangered species. In 2023, a very wet year, it received its full water allocation. Its auto tour routes and nature trails are free to visit, and about 8,200 people a year come for programs from waterfowl hunting to wildlife watching. The refuge, about 20 miles west of Delano, has its office on Corcoran Road.

places.name: Kern and Kings county line
places.text: The line between Kern and Kings counties crosses the freeway here. Kern County, formed in 1866, takes its name from the Kern River. Kings County, carved out of Tulare County in 1893, takes its name from the Kings River, which Spanish soldiers called the River of the Holy Kings.
places.more: Gabriel Moraga's Spanish expedition camped beside that river on January 6, 1806, the feast of the Epiphany, when Christians honor the three wise men, so they named it El Río de los Santos Reyes. After the United States took California in 1848, the name became the Kings River. Most of Tulare Lake lay in what is now Kings County, and about 87 percent of the county's land is farmland. In 2022 its most valuable product was milk, worth nearly a billion dollars, followed by pistachios, silage, processing tomatoes and cotton.

places.name: The Coastal Branch
places.text: A few miles west of here, a branch of the California Aqueduct splits off and heads for the coast. The Coastal Branch runs 116 miles, climbing through five pumping plants to deliver water to San Luis Obispo, Santa Maria and Santa Barbara.
places.more: The first 15 miles, an open canal, were finished in 1968. Most of the rest is a buried pipeline 42 to 57 inches across, built starting in 1994, which runs to a tank on Vandenberg Space Force Base. From there, an extension 42 miles long, finished in 1997, carries water through Lompoc, Buellton and Solvang to Lake Cachuma in the Los Padres National Forest. The pumping plants have names such as Las Perillas, Badger Hill, Devil's Den, Bluestone and Polonio Pass.

places.name: Alpaugh and Atwell's Island
places.text: Utica Avenue leads east to Alpaugh, a town on what was once Atwell's Island, the largest island in Tulare Lake. It was first known as Hog-Root Island, and a Visalia lawyer named Allen Atwell raised hogs on it. The island was a regular stop for the lake's commercial ferry.
places.more: Long before, the Wowol Yokuts village of Chawlowin stood on the island, and after 1852 Yokuts families who had been forced from their homes hid there among the tules. It is the last recorded place where Native people lived on the lake on their own, into the 1870s. Yoimut, who lived there as a child, later told how settlers put cattle on the island and the families left, afraid of being burned out. The town is named for John Alpaugh, an officer of the land colony that developed it, and oil and gas were found nearby in 1920 and 1921. When the lake came back in 2023, parts of Alpaugh were ordered to evacuate. The town's tap water carries too much arsenic, so residents rely on bottled water.

places.name: Colonel Allensworth's town
places.text: About 30 miles east, past Alpaugh, Colonel Allensworth State Historic Park preserves the first California town founded, financed and governed by African Americans. Army veteran Allen Allensworth and four partners started it in 1908, hoping to build a Tuskegee of the West, a place where Black families could own land, farm and run their own affairs.
places.more: Farmers grew alfalfa, wheat, sugar beets and cotton, and the town had a bakery, drugstore, hotel, library and a school that became California's first African American school district. Then troubles piled up. The water table dropped and alkali salts spread, the Santa Fe railroad moved its stop to Alpaugh in 1914, and that September, Colonel Allensworth was struck and killed by a motorcycle in Monrovia. Many residents left after World War I. A former resident, Ed Pope, led the push to save the site. The park was established in 1976, and its restored buildings include the schoolhouse, hotel and general store. Every year it hosts a Juneteenth celebration and a rededication event in October.

places.name: A landfill and a town's fight
places.text: Off Highway 41, about 3.5 miles southwest of Kettleman City, the Kettleman Hills facility is a landfill of about 1,500 acres for hazardous and household waste, run by a subsidiary of Waste Management. It opened in the late 1970s. In recent decades it has been the focus of an environmental justice fight in Kettleman City, a small, mostly Spanish-speaking farmworker town.
places.more: In 2007 and 2008, the environmental justice group Greenaction reported a cluster of birth defects and infant deaths in town and linked them to pollution sources in the area, including the landfill. When the company asked to expand, many of the town's roughly 1,500 residents fought it, fearing more PCB waste. The company says it passes its inspections and that no link to the birth defects has been established, and the state investigated. In 2014 state regulators approved the expansion and then denied two appeals, and opponents vowed to keep challenging it.

places.name: Crossing the California Aqueduct
places.text: The freeway crosses the California Aqueduct here, the concrete river that carries water from the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta toward Southern California. Counting from the south, this is the second of I-5's five crossings of the aqueduct. A typical stretch is 40 feet wide at the bottom and holds water about 30 feet deep, and the whole aqueduct runs more than 400 miles.
places.more: It is named for Governor Edmund G. Pat Brown and is the main feature of the State Water Project. It begins at Clifton Court Forebay in the Delta, where the first pumps lift the water 240 feet. North of Kettleman City the canal is the federally built San Luis Canal, which carries water for both the state and federal projects; it ends at Kettleman City, where the state-built aqueduct takes over. The aqueduct's widest section is 110 feet across, and it can carry 13,100 cubic feet of water a second. A 2021 study estimated that covering canals like this with solar panels could save 11 to 22 million gallons of water per mile each year from evaporation.
places.spot: Look for the wide concrete canal of the aqueduct passing under the freeway.

places.name: Ghost of Tulare Lake
places.text: East of here lies the bed of Tulare Lake, once the largest freshwater lake west of the Mississippi River. The Tachi Yokut Tribe calls it Pa'ashi, big water. The rivers that fed it were diverted for farming, and by 1899 it was dry except for marshes.
places.more: For thousands of years the lake supported perhaps the largest Native population north of Mexico, with the Tachi, Wowol and Chunut Yokuts living around its shores. In the late 1850s, settlers began killing or forcibly removing most of the Yokuts people here. The lake keeps coming back in flood years: in 1983 it took two years to dry out, and in 2023 storms brought back more than 114,000 acres of it, flooding farms and homes. Yoimut, a woman who spent much of her life on the lake, had warned that it would return. During World War II, Navy flying boats used it as a backup landing place. The Tachi Yokut Tribe is among those working to restore it for good.

places.name: Kettleman City, halfway
places.text: Kettleman City is near the halfway point between Los Angeles and San Francisco or Sacramento, which makes this exit a major stop for food and lodging. The travel stops cluster at the Highway 41 junction, while the town itself, about 1,200 people, sits about a mile north, past the aqueduct. It lies only about half a mile north of the 36th parallel.
places.more: A real estate developer, A. Manford Brown, founded the town in 1929, right after oil was found in the hills, and its main street, Highway 41, was named Brown Street after him. In the early 1900s, before Tulare Lake shrank, people traveled between Lemoore and Kettleman by ferry, and as the lake receded in the late 1920s, that route became Highway 41. By 1940 about 600 people lived here. The aqueduct and the freeway both arrived in the early 1970s, and farming on the West Side grew with the new water. Most residents speak Spanish at home, and many work in agriculture.

places.name: Kettleman Hills
places.text: The long, low hills along the west side are the Kettleman Hills, about 30 miles long and up to about 1,200 feet high. They are named, with a spelling change, for Dave Kettelman, who grazed sheep and cattle here in the 1860s. They are a long fold in the rock, squeezed up by tectonic forces, and they run parallel to the San Andreas Fault, farther west.
places.more: The range is really two long domes, the North Dome and the Middle Dome, and each sits on an oil field; the North Dome's field alone is about 14 miles long. Grass covers most of the hills, and summer highs regularly top 100 degrees. Before 1910, drillers tried nine times to reach oil here and failed, because their equipment could not drill the 7,000 feet needed. On August 4, 1985, an earthquake of about magnitude 6 caused slight damage in Avenal, Kettleman City, Hanford and Lemoore, and some scientists have suggested that decades of pumping oil out of these hills helped set it off.
places.spot: Look for a long line of low hills west of the freeway.

places.name: Avenal, the oat field
places.text: Highway 269 crosses the Kettleman Hills to Avenal, whose name is Spanish for oat field. Spanish soldiers and explorers named it for the wild oats, waist high, that covered the plain like golden silk. Standard Oil laid out the town in 1929, after oil was found in the hills, and its first post office was a cigar box on the counter of the general store.
places.more: Standard Oil built the town a 600-seat theater and a hospital, and by 1936 about 3,000 people lived here, mostly oil workers. When salt water seeped into the oil reservoir, production collapsed, and the town shrank until farmworkers arrived in the 1960s. After Avenal became a city, it asked the state for a prison, the first California prison a community actively sought. Avenal State Prison opened in 1987, and in 2019 its inmates made up about a third of the city's population. The city limits reach across the hills to take in this part of the freeway. Avenal also has a gliderport, one of the few airports in the western U.S. just for gliders.

places.name: The 1928 Kettleman gusher
places.text: In October 1928, after 19 months of drilling, the Milham Exploration Company's Elliott Number 1 well struck oil more than 7,000 feet under the Kettleman Hills. It blew out with a roar heard 20 miles away, spraying oil so light that it was white, and it reportedly could run a car without refining. The Kettleman North Dome became one of the most productive oil fields in the country.
places.more: The blowout took three years to bring under control, and thousands of spectators reportedly came to watch it. California had no limits on pumping, so Kettleman's flood of oil pushed prices down and caused bitter feelings in the oil industry. Production peaked in 1936 at more than 29 million barrels. In 1929, PG&E built a 300-mile pipeline from the field to San Francisco, which became the first major city to switch from manufactured gas to natural gas. Today less than half of one percent of the field's original oil is left. The 1940 movie Boom Town, with Clark Gable and Spencer Tracy, ends with their characters about to drill on the Kettleman Dome.

places.name: Garlic country
places.text: Fresno County grows most of the garlic in the United States, and west side towns such as Huron picked up the slack as Gilroy, once the country's biggest garlic producer, ran out of room. In 2022 the county harvested about 23,000 acres and 185,000 tons of garlic, nearly two-thirds of California's crop, worth about 350 million dollars.
places.more: Urban growth spreading from San Jose pushed most of the garlic out of Gilroy, and Santa Clara County, its home, was down to about 300 acres in one count. After the garlic is cut, it is left in the field to dry under its own tops, which come to look like straw. Fresno County's harvest has stayed huge for years: about 178,000 tons in 2020 and 187,000 tons in 2021. Worldwide, though, China grows nearly three-quarters of all garlic.

places.name: Gates Substation bottleneck
places.text: The sprawling electrical yard east of the freeway is Gates Substation, a key junction on the power lines linking Northern and Southern California. Between here and Los Banos, the corridor once had only two of its biggest lines. That bottleneck limited how much power could flow, and it was one of the leading causes of the California electricity crisis of 2000 and 2001.
places.more: Elsewhere the lines could carry about 5,400 megawatts from south to north, but between Los Banos and Gates only 3,900. The weak spot was flagged in the 1990s, but no one acted on it until after the crisis. The federal Western Area Power Administration and several utilities then built a third 500,000-volt line, finished on time and under budget on December 21, 2004, and Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger attended the commissioning ceremony. From Gates, one big line turns southwest across the Diablo Range toward the Diablo Canyon Power Plant on the coast.
places.spot: Look for a huge yard of electrical equipment and tall towers east of the freeway.

places.name: Huron, harvest town
places.text: East of the freeway is Huron, a farm town of about 6,200 people that swells to more than 15,000 at harvest time, when migrant farmworkers arrive. It began in 1888 as a water stop on the Southern Pacific Railroad. In the 2000 census, Huron had the highest share of Hispanic or Latino residents of any city in the United States.
places.more: Joseph Mouren and his family did much to grow the town in the late 1800s, and Mouren Drive is named for him. In the early 1900s Huron became one of the largest wool producers in the nation. During World War II, three training airstrips around town, Huron Field, West Field and Indian Field, served Lemoore Army Air Field. The town sits at 374 feet above sea level, about 15 miles east-northeast of Coalinga.

places.name: Arroyo Pasajero bridges
places.text: The freeway bridges here cross Los Gatos Creek, once called Arroyo Pasajero, the travelers' creek. On March 10, 1995, extreme rain sent fast floodwater down the creek. The flood scoured the creek bed and undermined the bridge piers, both I-5 bridges failed, and four cars and a truck went into the creek. Seven people died.
places.more: The creek starts in the Diablo Range near Benito Pass and flows past Coalinga into the valley. Its old waterhole, Poso de Chane, northwest of the Guijarral Hills, was the site of a Native village the Spanish called the Chane, and later a stop on El Camino Viejo, until the Great Flood of 1862 destroyed it. Engineers who studied the 1995 failure found that the flood had scoured the creek bed down around the bridge supports, and that the force of water and debris, striking the columns at an angle, broke them. Both of the bridges standing here today were built that same year.
places.spot: Look for the creek bed under the freeway bridges.

zones.label: Wheeler Ridge and the valley's edge
zones.text: Below the Grapevine the land flattens at Wheeler Ridge, where the Tehachapi and San Emigdio mountains meet the floor of the San Joaquin Valley and Highway 99 meets I-5.

seasons.winter: From November through March, thick tule fog can settle over the valley floor.
seasons.spring: In spring, Wind Wolves Preserve in the hills to the southwest holds a nature festival with guided hikes and wildflower viewing.

zones.label: The vanished southern lakes
zones.text: Flat farmland covers the old beds of Kern Lake and Buena Vista Lake, with the San Emigdio Mountains forming the valley's southern wall and the oil country of Maricopa and Taft off to the west.

zones.label: Kern County orchards
zones.text: Kern County's valley floor here is farm country, where almonds and pistachios are among the most valuable crops, and Highways 119 and 43 lead west to the oil towns of Taft and Maricopa.

zones.label: Kern River and the Elk Hills
zones.text: The freeway crosses the Kern River near the Kern Water Bank's recharge basins and runs past the low, bare Elk Hills, which sit on one of the country's great oil fields.

seasons.summer: Late summer is when the tule elk at the state reserve off Stockdale Highway become most active.
seasons.fall: The elk stay most active into early autumn.

zones.label: Buttonwillow cotton country
zones.text: Around Buttonwillow, known locally as cotton country, farm fields and big power lines spread across the valley floor, with the Temblor Range on the far western skyline.

seasons.winter: On calm winter nights from November through March, tule fog can cut visibility to a few hundred feet.

zones.label: Lost Hills oil and pistachios
zones.text: Oil pumps dot the low Lost Hills west of the freeway, the aqueduct runs past the town of Lost Hills, and Kern National Wildlife Refuge lies out on the flats to the east.

seasons.winter: In winter, Kern National Wildlife Refuge to the east shelters migrating ducks, geese and other water birds.
seasons.fall: Pistachio harvest comes in the fall, when the trees are shaken and the nuts hauled to processing plants.

zones.label: Into Kings County
zones.text: North of the Kern County line, the Kettleman Hills rise west of the freeway, while the old bed of Tulare Lake, now farmland, spreads to the east.

seasons.winter: In very wet winters, like 2023, storms can bring Tulare Lake back, flooding the old lakebed east of the freeway.

zones.label: Kettleman Hills
zones.text: The Kettleman Hills rise west of the freeway, above the oil field that gave rise to Kettleman City and Avenal.

zones.label: Fresno County's West Side
zones.text: The freeway runs through the West Side farmland of Fresno County, which in 2022 led California counties in the value of its almonds, pistachios, garlic and processing tomatoes.

trivia.q: Where does the name Grapevine come from?
choices: A winery at the bottom of the grade
trivia.why: In 1772 Pedro Fages named the canyon Cañada de las Uvas, the canyon of the grapes, for its wild California grapevines.

trivia.q: How high does the Edmonston Pumping Plant lift water to get it over the Tehachapi Mountains?
trivia.why: Edmonston lifts the water 1,926 feet, the most powerful water lift in the world apart from pumped-storage power plants.

trivia.q: How long did the 1910 Lakeview Gusher keep spilling oil?
trivia.why: It gushed for about 18 months and released roughly 9 million barrels of oil.

trivia.q: Before it was named for President Taft, what did the railroad call the station at Taft?
trivia.why: The railroad named it Moron because Moro might be confused with Morro Bay; it was renamed Taft in 1909.

trivia.q: In the 1870s, when tule elk were thought to be extinct, where were the last few found?
choices: On an island in San Francisco Bay
Hiding in the tules near Buena Vista Lake
On top of the Tehachapi Mountains
trivia.why: In 1874 a game warden, tipped off by Henry Miller, found the survivors hiding in the tules near Buena Vista Lake.

trivia.q: The tree that gave Buttonwillow its name is actually what kind of plant?
trivia.why: Despite the name, the landmark tree is a buttonbush, not a willow.

trivia.q: What has stayed within about 10 miles of Buttonwillow since 1970?
choices: The hottest spot in the state
trivia.why: The Census Bureau's center of population for California, the point where a map of all its people would balance, has stayed within about 10 miles of Buttonwillow since 1970.

trivia.q: The Temblor Range on the western skyline is named for a Spanish word. What does temblor mean?
trivia.why: Temblor is Spanish for tremor, fitting for mountains beside the San Andreas Fault.

trivia.q: What were the drillers looking for when they found the Lost Hills oil field in 1910?
trivia.why: They were drilling a water well for livestock and struck oil at 530 feet.

trivia.q: Kettleman City is close to the halfway point between Los Angeles and which city?
trivia.why: Exit 309 sits near the halfway point between Los Angeles and San Francisco or Sacramento.

trivia.q: Tulare Lake, east of Kettleman City, was once what?
choices: A salty bay of the Pacific Ocean
A crater lake in an old volcano
The largest freshwater lake west of the Mississippi River
A reservoir built for the aqueduct
trivia.why: Tulare Lake was once the largest freshwater lake west of the Mississippi; it was drained for farming but returns in very wet years.

trivia.q: The name Avenal comes from Spanish. What does it mean?
trivia.why: Spanish soldiers and explorers named it for the wild oats that covered the plain.
